End-to-end calibration validation: after calibration, sweep the input across the full range at -40C, 25C, and 85C, and verify the error stays within the accuracy spec at every point. If the error exceeds spec at temperature extremes, the temperature compensation model needs more terms (higher-order polynomial or a lookup table with finer temperature resolution).

description: Design a wireless communication system from link budget analysis through modulation selection, RF front-end design, antenna selection, and protocol implementation for ISM-band applications.

steps.description: Calculate the complete link budget to determine whether the required range is achievable with the available transmit power and receiver sensitivity.

inputs.name: system-requirements
inputs.desc: Required range, data rate, BER target, operating frequency band (915 MHz, 2.4 GHz, etc.), environment (indoor, outdoor, urban, rural)

inputs.name: regulatory-limits
inputs.desc: Maximum EIRP from regulations (FCC Part 15: +30 dBm for 902-928 MHz, +20 dBm for 2.4 GHz ISM)

outputs.name: link-budget-table
outputs.desc: Complete link budget from transmitter to receiver: Tx power, antenna gains, path loss, fade margin, cable losses, and resulting received power vs receiver sensitivity

outputs.name: link-margin
outputs.desc: The margin between received power and sensitivity, which must be positive by at least the fade margin (typically 10 to 20 dB for outdoor, 20 to 30 dB for indoor with multipath)

process: Free-space path loss (FSPL): FSPL(dB) = 20*log10(d) + 20*log10(f) + 32.45 where d is distance in km and f is frequency in MHz. At 2.4 GHz and 100 meters: FSPL = 20*log10(0.1) + 20*log10(2400) + 32.45 = -20 + 67.6 + 32.45 = 80 dB. At 915 MHz and 1 km: FSPL = 0 + 59.2 + 32.45 = 91.7 dB.

Add environment-specific losses. Indoor: wall penetration loss (5 to 15 dB per wall depending on material: drywall 3 dB, concrete 10 dB, metal 20+ dB), floor penetration (10 to 20 dB per floor). Outdoor urban: Hata model or Okumura-Hata for distances beyond 1 km. Vegetation: 0.2 dB/m for foliage at 2.4 GHz.

Fade margin accounts for multipath fading (constructive and destructive interference from reflected signals) and shadowing (obstruction by moving objects). For 99 percent link availability in a Rayleigh fading environment, the fade margin must be 20 dB. For 99.9 percent: 30 dB. Indoor environments with strong multipath need higher margins.

Received power: Prx(dBm) = Ptx(dBm) + Gtx(dBi) - Lcable_tx(dB) - FSPL(dB) - Lmisc(dB) + Grx(dBi) - Lcable_rx(dB). The link margin is: Margin = Prx - Sensitivity - Fade_margin. If margin is negative, the link cannot close at the required range. Options: increase Tx power (up to regulatory limit), increase antenna gain (larger antenna), reduce data rate (improves sensitivity), or reduce range.

Sensitivity is set by the required Eb/N0 for the modulation and coding at the target BER: Sensitivity(dBm) = -174 + 10*log10(BW) + NF + Eb/N0_required where -174 dBm/Hz is the thermal noise floor at 290K, BW is the receiver noise bandwidth in Hz, and NF is the receiver noise figure in dB. For BLE (1 MHz BW, NF = 6 dB, GFSK with Eb/N0 = 10 dB for BER 1e-3): Sensitivity = -174 + 60 + 6 + 10 = -98 dBm.

steps.description: Design the RF front end including the LNA, mixer, filters, and PA to meet the sensitivity and linearity requirements from the link budget.

inputs.name: link-budget-table
inputs.desc: Required sensitivity, maximum input power (for blocker scenarios), and transmit power

inputs.name: frequency-band
inputs.desc: Center frequency, bandwidth, adjacent channel rejection requirement

outputs.name: receiver-chain
outputs.desc: LNA noise figure and gain, mixer conversion loss and IIP3, IF/baseband filter bandwidth, and overall receiver noise figure and dynamic range

outputs.name: transmitter-chain
outputs.desc: PA output power, efficiency (PAE), linearity (EVM, ACPR), harmonic filtering

process: Cascaded noise figure (Friis equation): NF_total = NF1 + (NF2 - 1)/G1 + (NF3 - 1)/(G1*G2) + ... where NF and G are in linear (not dB). The LNA dominates the overall noise figure if its gain is high enough. For NF_total < 3 dB: choose an LNA with NF < 1.5 dB and gain > 15 dB, so the mixer noise contribution (NF2-1)/G1 < 1 dB even with a high-loss mixer.

LNA selection: key parameters are noise figure, gain, IIP3 (input third-order intercept point), and current consumption. For 2.4 GHz: typical integrated LNAs achieve NF = 1 to 2 dB, gain = 15 to 20 dB, IIP3 = -10 to 0 dBm. The LNA must not saturate from strong nearby transmitters; the maximum input without compression is P1dB_input = IIP3 - 9.6 dB.

Mixer selection: for superheterodyne, the mixer converts RF to IF. Conversion loss is typically 6 to 8 dB for passive mixers (no gain, but excellent linearity with IIP3 > +15 dBm) and -10 to -15 dB (gain) for active mixers (worse linearity with IIP3 around -5 dBm). For direct-conversion (zero-IF), the mixer converts directly to baseband, eliminating the IF filter but introducing DC offset and 1/f noise challenges.

System IIP3 (cascaded): 1/IIP3_total = 1/IIP3_1 + G1/IIP3_2 + G1*G2/IIP3_3 + ... The last stage before the ADC typically dominates the linearity because it sees the highest signal level. Design the gain distribution so that the signal level at each stage stays well below that stage's P1dB.

PA design for the transmitter: the required output power from the link budget sets the PA power rating. Power-added efficiency PAE = (Pout - Pin) / Pdc is the key figure of merit. Class A: PAE up to 50 percent but typically 25 to 35 percent. Class AB: 40 to 60 percent. Class E/F (switching mode): 60 to 80 percent but only for constant-envelope modulations (FSK, GMSK). For non-constant-envelope modulations (QAM, OFDM), back off the PA by 6 to 10 dB from P1dB to meet EVM and spectral mask requirements.

steps.description: Select or design the antenna to meet the gain, bandwidth, size, and polarization requirements for the wireless system.

inputs.name: link-budget-table
inputs.desc: Required antenna gain (Tx and Rx), operating frequency and bandwidth

inputs.name: physical-constraints
inputs.desc: Available volume, ground plane size, mounting (PCB trace, external, chip antenna), polarization requirement

outputs.name: antenna-selection
outputs.desc: Antenna type (PCB trace, chip, wire, patch, helical), dimensions, gain pattern, return loss (S11 < -10 dB across the band), and efficiency

outputs.name: matching-network
outputs.desc: Impedance matching components (LC network) to transform the antenna impedance to 50 ohm at the operating frequency

process: Antenna size scales with wavelength. At 2.4 GHz, lambda = 12.5 cm, so a quarter-wave monopole is 3.1 cm. At 915 MHz, lambda = 33 cm, so a quarter-wave monopole is 8.2 cm. If the available space is smaller than lambda/4, the antenna will be electrically small and the efficiency drops (radiation resistance decreases while loss resistance stays constant).

PCB trace antenna (inverted-F, meandered monopole): zero additional cost, 0 to 2 dBi gain, but requires a ground plane clearance area (no copper pour) of at least lambda/4 x lambda/10 around the antenna. The ground plane IS part of the antenna; its size and shape affect the radiation pattern and impedance. Minimum ground plane size for reasonable efficiency: lambda/4 x lambda/4.

Chip antenna (ceramic): compact (3 to 8 mm), 0 to 1 dBi gain, requires a matching network and specific ground plane keep-out per the manufacturer's datasheet. Less efficient than a well-designed PCB trace antenna but easier to implement. The matching network (pi or L network of capacitors and inductors) tunes the antenna impedance to 50 ohm; the component values are frequency-specific and must be verified on the actual PCB.

Patch antenna: directional (6 to 9 dBi gain in the broadside direction), useful when the communication partner is in a known direction. Size is lambda/2 x lambda/2 (6 cm x 6 cm at 2.4 GHz). Bandwidth is narrow (1 to 5 percent for a standard patch; wider with stacked or slotted designs). Polarization is set by the feed point location (linear) or with two feeds in quadrature (circular).

Impedance matching: measure the antenna impedance with a VNA (vector network analyzer) on the actual PCB (not on a test board, because the ground plane affects impedance). Design an L-network or pi-network to transform the measured impedance to 50 ohm. The matching bandwidth determines the usable frequency range: a narrowband match (high Q) gives better efficiency at the center frequency but less bandwidth.

description: Design protection circuits for electronic systems covering ESD, overvoltage, reverse polarity, inrush current limiting, overcurrent, hot-swap, and surge protection to meet safety and reliability standards.

steps.description: Design ESD protection for all external-facing pins to survive the ESD events specified by the applicable standard without damaging the protected IC.

inputs.name: esd-standard
inputs.desc: Target ESD withstand level (IEC 61000-4-2: contact 4kV/air 8kV for Level 2, contact 8kV/air 15kV for Level 4; HBM: 2kV or 4kV; CDM: 500V or 1kV)

inputs.name: protected-pins
inputs.desc: List of external pins with their signal type (digital I/O, analog input, power), operating voltage, data rate, and capacitance tolerance

outputs.name: esd-devices
outputs.desc: TVS diode or ESD protection IC for each pin: working voltage, clamping voltage at specified current, capacitance, and package

outputs.name: pcb-layout-rules
outputs.desc: Routing rules for ESD paths: TVS placement distance from connector, trace width, ground connection strategy

process: Select TVS diode working voltage: Vrwm (reverse working voltage) must exceed the maximum signal voltage by at least 10 percent. For a 3.3V digital signal: Vrwm >= 3.6V, so select a 5V TVS. The clamping voltage Vc at the specified peak pulse current (e.g., 16A for IEC 61000-4-2 at 8kV contact) must be below the protected IC's absolute maximum rating.

Capacitance matters for high-speed signals. A standard TVS diode adds 50 to 500 pF, which is acceptable for power and low-speed I/O but degrades signal integrity on USB, HDMI, or Ethernet. For high-speed lines, use low-capacitance TVS arrays (0.5 to 5 pF) or rail-clamp ESD protection ICs designed for the specific interface.

PCB layout is critical for ESD protection effectiveness. The TVS must be placed as close as possible to the connector pin, before the signal trace reaches the protected IC. The ground connection from the TVS must be short (under 10mm) and wide (at least 20 mil) with a direct via to the ground plane. A long ground trace adds inductance that increases the voltage at the protected IC during the fast ESD transient.

For multi-pin connectors, use a TVS array IC that protects all pins in one package, sharing a common ground. This saves board space and ensures matched protection across all pins. For differential pairs (USB, Ethernet), use TVS arrays specifically designed for differential signals that clamp both common-mode and differential ESD events.

Verify protection by ESD testing to the target standard. IEC 61000-4-2 testing uses a specified ESD generator (150 pF, 330 ohm for contact discharge) applied to each external pin. Verify that the equipment continues to operate (performance criterion A) or recovers after reset (criterion B) after the specified number of discharges (typically 10 positive and 10 negative per pin).

steps.description: Design protection against sustained overvoltage on the power input and reverse polarity connection, without excessive voltage drop or power loss during normal operation.

inputs.name: input-voltage-range
inputs.desc: Normal operating voltage range (e.g., 9 to 36V for automotive), maximum expected overvoltage (e.g., load dump 60V for 40ms in automotive), reverse voltage

inputs.name: current-range
inputs.desc: Normal operating current, maximum load current

outputs.name: overvoltage-circuit
outputs.desc: Protection topology (crowbar, clamp, foldback), component values, and the voltage seen by the downstream circuit during an overvoltage event

outputs.name: reverse-polarity-circuit
outputs.desc: Protection topology (series diode, P-FET, ideal diode controller), voltage drop and power dissipation during normal operation

process: Reverse polarity with a series diode: simple but wastes Vf * Iload (0.3 to 0.7V * current) continuously. A Schottky diode reduces Vf to 0.3V but leaks more reverse current at high temperature. For currents above 1A, the loss becomes significant.

Reverse polarity with a P-channel MOSFET: the MOSFET body diode conducts during normal polarity (Vgs = -Vin, turning on the FET), and blocks during reverse polarity (Vgs = 0, FET off). Forward voltage drop is I*Rds_on, typically 10 to 50 mV at rated current. This is 10 to 50x lower loss than a diode. The FET must be rated for the full reverse voltage on Vds.

Overvoltage clamp: a TVS diode across the input clamps transient overvoltage. For automotive load dump (ISO 7637-2 pulse 5: 60V for 400ms), the TVS must absorb significant energy: E = integral(V*I*dt). A 36V working voltage TVS clamping at 50V with 1A load for 400ms absorbs about 20 J, which exceeds most discrete TVS ratings. Use a series resistor to limit current, or use a dedicated transient voltage suppressor module.

For sustained overvoltage protection, an active clamp or a DC-DC converter with wide input range is more appropriate than a TVS. An active clamp uses a series FET that enters linear mode to regulate the output voltage when the input exceeds a threshold, dissipating the excess voltage as heat. The FET must survive the SOA (safe operating area) at the overvoltage condition.

Crowbar protection: a thyristor (SCR) fires when the voltage exceeds a threshold (set by a zener trigger), short-circuiting the input and blowing the upstream fuse. This is destructive (fuse must be replaced) but protects against high-energy overvoltage. Used in military and aerospace where the protected circuit is more valuable than the fuse.

steps.description: Design the hot-swap and inrush current limiting circuit for boards inserted into a live backplane, protecting both the board and the backplane from damage.

inputs.name: bus-voltage
inputs.desc: Backplane voltage (12V, 48V, etc.), allowed voltage transient on the bus during insertion

inputs.name: load-capacitance
inputs.desc: Total capacitance on the board that must be charged during insertion (bulk capacitors, MLCC, etc.)

inputs.name: steady-state-current
inputs.desc: Normal operating current after the board is fully inserted and powered

outputs.name: hot-swap-circuit
outputs.desc: Hot-swap controller IC, series MOSFET (rating and SOA verification), sense resistor, and timing capacitor for dV/dt and current limiting

outputs.name: soa-analysis
outputs.desc: FET safe operating area plot showing the insertion transient trajectory (voltage across FET vs current through FET vs time) stays within the SOA boundary

process: During insertion, the board's bulk capacitance is at 0V while the backplane is at Vbus. Without limiting, the inrush current is I_peak = Vbus / (R_connector + R_trace), which can be hundreds of amps for a low-impedance bus. This current can weld connector pins, cause a bus voltage dip affecting other boards, and damage capacitors.

A series N-channel MOSFET controlled by a hot-swap controller limits the inrush current by operating in the linear region during startup. The controller ramps the gate voltage slowly (controlled by an external capacitor on the GATE pin), which limits dV/dt across the load capacitance: dV/dt = I_limit / C_load. The charging time is t_charge = C_load * Vbus / I_limit.

Current limiting: a sense resistor in series with the MOSFET source provides current feedback to the controller. When the current exceeds the limit (set by the controller's threshold voltage divided by the sense resistor), the controller reduces the gate voltage to maintain constant current. Typical I_limit = V_threshold / R_sense, e.g., 50mV / 10 mohm = 5A.

FET SOA verification: during the inrush event, the FET simultaneously carries the limit current and blocks (Vbus - V_load). The power dissipation is P = I_limit * (Vbus - V_load), which is maximum at the start (V_load = 0, so P = I_limit * Vbus). The FET must survive this power for the duration of the charging event. Plot the I_limit, Vds trajectory on the FET's SOA curve and verify it stays within the DC or pulsed SOA boundary for the charging duration.

After the load capacitance is charged and the FET is fully on (Vds = I_load * Rds_on), the hot-swap controller monitors for overcurrent and short circuit faults. An overcurrent fault (current exceeding the limit for a programmable time) triggers the controller to turn off the FET, disconnecting the board. A fast comparator detects short circuits (current exceeding 2 to 3x the limit) and turns off the FET within microseconds.

description: Design for electromagnetic compatibility by identifying EMI sources, measuring and mitigating conducted and radiated emissions, designing PCB layouts for EMC, and verifying compliance with CISPR 32 or FCC Part 15B.

steps.description: Identify and characterize all EMI sources in the system before designing mitigation, because fixing the source is always cheaper than filtering after the fact.

inputs.name: system-block-diagram
inputs.desc: All active blocks: switching converters, digital clocks, motor drives, communication interfaces, and their operating frequencies, edge rates, and current levels

inputs.name: emc-standard
inputs.desc: The applicable emissions standard (CISPR 32 Class B for residential, FCC Part 15 Class B, automotive: CISPR 25) with its frequency range and limits

outputs.name: emi-source-inventory
outputs.desc: For each source: fundamental frequency, harmonic spectrum estimate, current or voltage amplitude, and the coupling mechanism (conducted, radiated, or both)

outputs.name: risk-ranking
outputs.desc: Sources ranked by their likely contribution to emissions failure, based on amplitude and frequency relative to the limit

process: Switching power converters generate conducted DM noise at the switching frequency and its harmonics, plus CM noise from the switch node dV/dt coupling through parasitic capacitance to the chassis/ground. A buck converter switching at 500 kHz with 10 ns edges generates significant spectral energy up to 1/(pi*10ns) = 32 MHz.

Digital clocks generate radiated emissions from the PCB traces acting as unintentional antennas. A 100 MHz clock with 1 ns edges radiates harmonics up to 300 MHz or higher. The emission amplitude from a trace of length L carrying current I at frequency f is approximately: E = 1.3e-6 * f^2 * I * A / r (V/m) where A is the loop area (trace + return path) in m^2 and r is the distance in meters.

Motor drives generate broadband EMI from the PWM switching of the inverter. The motor cable acts as an antenna, radiating the PWM spectral content. CM current flows through the motor frame parasitic capacitance to ground. The EMI spectrum extends from the PWM frequency (typically 10 to 20 kHz) to tens of MHz.

Estimate the conducted emissions spectrum by calculating the Fourier coefficients of the switching waveform. For a trapezoidal waveform with amplitude A, duty cycle D, rise time tr, and frequency f0: the nth harmonic amplitude is An = 2*A*D*sinc(n*pi*D)*sinc(n*pi*f0*tr). Plot this envelope against the applicable limit line. The frequency range where the envelope exceeds the limit is where filtering is needed.

Rank sources by margin to limit. A source that exceeds the limit by 20 dB needs 20 dB of attenuation from filtering, shielding, or layout improvement. Sources within 6 dB of the limit are at risk due to measurement uncertainty and production variation. Sources more than 10 dB below the limit can typically be ignored.

steps.description: Design the EMI filter to reduce conducted emissions on the power input below the applicable limit, handling both differential-mode and common-mode noise.

inputs.name: emi-source-inventory
inputs.desc: Conducted emissions spectrum from each source, separated into DM and CM components

inputs.name: emc-standard
inputs.desc: Conducted emissions limit line (e.g., CISPR 32 Class B: quasi-peak and average limits from 150 kHz to 30 MHz)

outputs.name: filter-design
outputs.desc: Schematic of the EMI filter with component values: X-capacitors, Y-capacitors, common-mode choke, and DM inductor (or choke leakage inductance)

outputs.name: filter-performance
outputs.desc: Predicted insertion loss vs frequency for both DM and CM, showing adequate margin to the limit at all frequencies

process: DM filter: X-capacitors shunt DM noise to the return conductor. A single X-cap provides -20 dB/decade above its self-resonant frequency. For more attenuation, use an LC pi-filter: X-cap, DM inductor, X-cap. Each LC stage provides -40 dB/decade above the resonant frequency. The DM inductor can be a separate component or the leakage inductance of the CM choke.

CM filter: Y-capacitors shunt CM noise from each line to the chassis ground. A CM choke (two windings on one core, wound in the same direction) presents high impedance to CM current and near-zero impedance to DM current. The CM choke impedance is: Zcm = 2*pi*f*Lcm up to the self-resonant frequency, then decreases. Select a choke with self-resonant frequency above the highest frequency where CM attenuation is needed.

Y-capacitor value is limited by safety leakage current. For IEC 60950-1 Class I equipment: total leakage through Y-caps must be under 3.5 mA at maximum line voltage and frequency. At 240 VAC, 50 Hz: C_y_max = 3.5e-3 / (2*pi*50*240) = 46 nF total. Typical values are 2.2 nF to 4.7 nF per line-to-ground Y-cap.

Damping: the filter LC resonance can amplify noise at the resonant frequency instead of attenuating it. Add damping to prevent resonance peaks that exceed the limit. A resistor in series with a capacitor across the filter input (Rd, Cd network) damps the resonance. Rd is chosen to equal the characteristic impedance sqrt(L/C) of the filter at resonance. Cd must be at least 4x the filter capacitor to be effective.

Verify the filter by measuring conducted emissions with a LISN (line impedance stabilization network) per the applicable standard. The LISN provides a defined 50 ohm impedance at the measurement port and isolates the equipment under test from the mains. Compare the measured emissions against the quasi-peak and average limits. If the measured emissions exceed the limit at any frequency, increase the filter attenuation at that frequency by adding components or improving layout.

steps.description: Apply PCB layout techniques to minimize radiated emissions and improve immunity, because layout errors cause more EMC failures than missing filters.

inputs.name: system-block-diagram
inputs.desc: Block placement, signal routing requirements, power distribution

inputs.name: risk-ranking
inputs.desc: EMI sources ranked by contribution to emissions

outputs.name: layout-rules
outputs.desc: Specific layout rules for this design: ground plane strategy, high-speed signal routing, power loop minimization, connector placement, and shield grounding

outputs.name: layout-review-checklist
outputs.desc: A checklist of EMC-critical layout items to verify before fabrication

process: Minimize loop area for all high-frequency current paths. Every current flows in a loop (outgoing path + return path). The loop radiates as a magnetic dipole: E proportional to f^2 * I * A where A is the loop area. For a switching converter, the hot loop (switch, inductor, capacitor, return) must be as small as possible. Place the input capacitor directly adjacent to the switch with the shortest trace length.

Provide a continuous ground plane on at least one inner layer. The ground plane provides a low-impedance return path for all signals. High-frequency return current flows directly under the signal trace (path of least inductance), so a continuous plane under the signal trace keeps the loop area equal to the trace length times the dielectric thickness (small). Any slot or gap in the ground plane forces the return current to detour around the gap, creating a large loop that radiates.

Route high-speed signals on inner layers (stripline) when possible. Stripline is shielded by ground planes above and below, reducing radiated emissions by 20+ dB compared to microstrip on an outer layer. If microstrip must be used, keep the traces short and away from board edges (edge radiation).

Separate analog, digital, and power sections physically. Place the switching converter as far as possible from sensitive analog circuits. Route the switching converter's hot loop on the side of the board closest to the ground plane. Never route a high-speed digital signal under or near an analog signal trace.

Ground stitching vias: place ground vias every lambda/20 around the board perimeter and around any ground plane split to prevent slot antenna effects. At 1 GHz (lambda = 30 cm), this means a via every 15 mm. Along the edge of a shield can or connector ground pad, vias should be spaced even closer (lambda/40) to provide a low-impedance connection to the ground plane.
